context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda` arm in `eval`, why does creating a lambda whose body references a nonexistent variable not return an error, and when would that unbound variable error actually occur?
probes.reason: Directly asks the student to explain why the `Lambda` arm never errors on unbound variables and identifies the exact moment the error would surface instead.

probes.question: Your code returns `Ok(VFunc(UserFn("lambda", params, body, env)))` without calling `eval` on `body`. If `body` has a typo in a variable name, why does this line still succeed, and what event would trigger the error?
probes.reason: Provides an alternate code-focused angle referencing the returned constructor to assess understanding of deferred body evaluation versus call-time evaluation.

content: In your `Lambda` arm in `eval`, why does creating a lambda whose body references a nonexistent variable not return an error, and when would that unbound variable error actually occur?

creating a lambda does not evaluate its body it only creates a function that captures its surrounding environment the unbound variable error occures when the lambda is called and its body is evaluated if the referenced variable cannot be found in the function environment

topic: lambda evaluation and deferred body execution
reason: The student correctly explains that creating a lambda does not evaluate its body, and that the unbound variable error occurs when the lambda is actually called and evaluated in its environment.
